local.levelRationale: Anchored on the headline: NYC discharges approximately 18 billion gallons a year of untreated combined sewage through 398 permitted CSO outfalls into a eutrophication- and pathogen-sensitive estuary, and the binding abatement commitment is only 1.67 billion gallons a year — roughly 9% of that load — on a deadline that has already slid from 2030 to December 2040 with a December 2045 backstop. Pushed up by three well-sourced shortfalls named individually: the Flushing Bay CSO control tunnel is now scheduled for construction completion in Q4 2053 at $3.42B (from $683M and 2035 in the approved LTCP); green/managed acreage stands at 2,062 acres against the ~8,000 acres implied by the 10%-of-impervious 2030 goal, and DEP missed the 1.5%-by-2015 and 4%-by-2020 application-rate milestones outright; and citywide WRRF effluent nitrogen is ~132,200 lb/day (~21,900 t N/yr, ~2.6 kg N/person/yr), roughly half of per-capita excreted nitrogen, meaning the city removes only about half the nitrogen it collects. Pulled down — but only as a modifier, per R12, not as the anchor — by three genuinely met nutrient targets: the Long Island Sound point-source load is 68% below the TMDL baseline against a 60% requirement (18,909 lb/day, 2025); Jamaica Bay WRRF nitrogen is ~17,100 lb/day against ~40,000 in early 2010, a ~57% cut against a >50% target; and harbor-wide summer dissolved oxygen has exceeded the NYS 5.0 mg/L standard every summer since the 1990s. Also pulled down modestly by DEP certifying its December 2025 consent-order milestone (668 MGY of CSO reduction, $1.4B encumbered) on time, on 30 December 2025. Not scored lower because meeting one's own consent order is not the same as living within planetary means: nitrogen is among the most-transgressed planetary boundaries (~190 Tg N/yr against a 62 Tg boundary), and a chronic multi-billion-gallon untreated discharge with a 2053 fix date is not inside the safe space.
local.indicator: Combined sewer overflow (CSO) annual discharge volume
local.value: Approximately 18 billion gallons of combined sewage discharged citywide per year through 398 permitted CSO outfalls; approximately 60% of the city's sewer system is combined. This is NYSDEC's published modelled average-year estimate and carries no stated vintage; DEP's LTCP modelling is normalised to the 'average rainfall year of 2008' and DEP publishes no measured citywide annual total.
local.target: Reduce CSO volume by 1.67 billion gallons per year by December 2040 for the average rainfall year of 2008, with $3.5B in green infrastructure encumbered by December 2040 and expended by December 2045 (2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Modification, DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38, effective 29 June 2023, modifying the 2005 CSO Order CO2-20000107-8). Interim milestones: 668 MGY / $1.4B encumbered by December 2025; 700-800 MGY / $1.8B by December 2030; 850-1,220 MGY / $2.8B by December 2035.
local.context: This is a wastewater-and-CSO story, not an agricultural-runoff story — the sharp structural contrast with Petaluma, where the same dimension is scored on groundwater nitrate near farms and septic systems. NYC's 14 water resource recovery facilities process about 1.3 billion gallons a day, and 12 of those 14 sewersheds are combined-sewered, containing 398-418 permitted CSO outfalls (DEC's current figure is 398; DEC's 2021 CSO Annual Report says 400 across the 12 combined sewersheds; the 2023 consent order itself recites 'approximately 418'; DEP's website's figure of 700 is a broader count of combined-sewer outfalls, not a superseded CSO count). Nitrogen and pathogen loading are therefore concentrated at engineered point sources tied to rain events, not diffuse land-based leaching. The nitrogen side of this dimension has genuinely succeeded: about $1.2B was spent between 1999 and 2022 upgrading 8 plants for biological nitrogen removal, and the Long Island Sound and Jamaica Bay nutrient targets are both met. The CSO side has not: ~$5.3B was spent on CSO and green infrastructure between 1995 and 2024 with ~$7.4B more programmed for 2025-2050, yet the committed reduction is only 1.67 BGY and the major grey projects run past mid-century. Caveat on the headline: DEP's 16 December 2025 Flushing Bay presentation shows an 'Untreated CSO Volume Reduction' graphic labelled 5.6 BGY (Baseline CSO & GI Program, $6.2B) and 3.5 BGY (LTCP CSO Program, $8.7B) which could not be reconciled with the 18 BGY figure from the extracted slide text; whether 18 BGY is a pre-programme baseline or a current modelled volume is unresolved.
local.source: NYSDEC 'New York City CSO Program' and statewide CSO pages (citing NYC DEP data); 2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Order on Consent (DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38); NYC DEP 'State of the Sewers 2024'

bronx.note: No borough-level CSO volume is published. DEP and DEC report CSO volumes by waterbody, and Bronx waterbodies span jurisdictions (the Bronx River and Hutchinson River LTCPs, plus Bronx-side outfalls counted under the Citywide/East River Open Waters LTCP). PROXY, measuring a different quantity than the headline: the Hunts Point WRRF (NY0026191, Bronx) discharged a CY2025 mean of ~6,633 lb/day total nitrogen (EPA ECHO DMRs, parameter 00600, Effluent Gross, monthly average). That is a nitrogen load, not a CSO volume, and it is assigned by plant location — Hunts Point discharges to the East River, whose loading is shared with Queens and Manhattan. The 2025 green-infrastructure certification records 78.0 green/managed acres and 25.4 MGY of CSO reduction in the Bronx River drainage and 66.4 acres / 35.8 MGY in the Hutchinson River drainage.
bronx.source: EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports; NYC DEP 2025 green infrastructure milestone certification

brooklyn.note: No borough-level CSO volume is published. PROXIES, each measuring a different quantity than the headline: (1) the four Brooklyn WRRFs discharged CY2025 means of ~2,617 lb/day (26th Ward, NY0026212), ~8,108 (Coney Island, NY0026182), ~26,342 (Newtown Creek, NY0026204), ~14,633 (Owls Head, NY0026166) and ~4,801 (Red Hook, NY0027073) total nitrogen — nitrogen loads, not CSO volumes, and assigned by plant location: 26th Ward and Coney Island discharge to Jamaica Bay, which borders Queens as well, and Newtown Creek WRRF discharges to the East River. (2) The Gowanus Canal receives an estimated 659 million gallons/year of CSO under its approved LTCP baseline, which is modelled for the 2008 average/typical rainfall year. (3) The 26th Ward carbon-addition facility, completed in February 2012 at ~$2M, cut >3,000 lb/day of nitrogen, then about 10% of total Jamaica Bay loading. Note also that 26th Ward is in Significant/Category I Noncompliance on its permit, with 9 quarters of SNC and copper, TSS, silver and whole-effluent-toxicity exceedances — a chemical-pollution issue rather than a nutrient one, flagged for the chemical pollution dimension.
brooklyn.source: EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports and detailed facility report; NYC DEP press release 7 Feb 2012; Gowanus Canal LTCP

manhattan.note: No borough-level CSO volume is published. PROXY, measuring a different quantity than the headline: Manhattan's two WRRFs discharged CY2025 means of ~19,067 lb/day (North River, NY0026247, to the Hudson) and ~14,542 lb/day (Wards Island, NY0026131, to the upper East River) total nitrogen. Assigned by plant location and materially misleading if read as Manhattan's load: Wards Island sits on Randall's Island and discharges to the upper East River, a reach shared with Queens and the Bronx and tributary to Long Island Sound. Historical context: Save the Sound reported in March 2013 that the Wards Island nitrogen upgrade cut discharge from 33,000 to 17,000 lb/day; the CY2025 figure is lower still.
manhattan.source: EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports; Save the Sound (2013) for historical context

queens.note: No borough-level CSO volume is published. PROXIES, each measuring a different quantity than the headline: (1) Queens WRRFs discharged CY2025 means of ~11,642 lb/day (Bowery Bay, NY0026158), ~4,892 (Tallman Island, NY0026239), ~5,158 (Jamaica, NY0026115) and ~1,242 (Rockaway, NY0026221) total nitrogen. Bowery Bay and Tallman Island are East River/Long Island Sound dischargers; Jamaica and Rockaway discharge to Jamaica Bay, shared with Brooklyn. (2) Capital status: the approved 2017 Flushing Bay LTCP requires a 25 million gallon CSO storage tunnel capturing outfalls BB-006 and BB-008; DEP's proposed December 2025 modification would instead deliver 6.5 MG of in-line storage (construction complete Q2 2037) plus a 40 MG tunnel (construction complete Q4 2053) at a combined $3.42B, versus $683M and 2035 in the 2016 LTCP. The modification request was submitted to DEC on 31 December 2025 and was still under DEC review as of the Q1 2026 quarterly report. (3) Flushing Bay and Flushing Creek together account for 323.4 green/managed acres and 162.4 MGY of certified CSO reduction, the largest outside Jamaica Bay.
queens.source: EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports; NYC DEP Flushing Bay LTCP CSO Tunnel public meeting, 16 Dec 2025; NYC DEP 2026 Q1 CSO quarterly report

statenIsland.note: No borough-level CSO volume is published, and there is no Staten Island waterbody LTCP among the 10 waterbody plans plus 1 citywide plan. IMPORTANT CORRECTION TO A COMMON CLAIM: Staten Island is NOT largely separately sewered — it is split roughly in half. The Oakwood Beach WRRF sewershed (NY0026174; 10,779-acre drainage area, ~245,000 people, southern and eastern Staten Island) is not a combined system and has no CSO outfalls, per DEC's 2021 CSO Annual Report. The Port Richmond WRRF sewershed (NY0026107; 9,665-acre drainage area, ~200,000 people, north shore) treats combined sewage and does have CSO outfalls. By drainage acreage that is about 47% combined / 53% separate; by served population about 45% / 55%. The Bluebelt program — ~10,000 acres across 16 watersheds using natural drainage corridors — sits within the already-separately-sewered southern and eastern part of the island, so it explains stormwater management there rather than explaining an absence of CSOs borough-wide. PROXY, measuring a different quantity than the headline: the two Staten Island WRRFs discharged CY2025 means of ~9,017 lb/day (Oakwood Beach) and ~3,550 lb/day (Port Richmond) total nitrogen.
statenIsland.source: NYSDEC Combined Sewer Overflows 2021 Annual Report; NYSDEC Port Richmond and Oakwood Beach WRRF permit records; NYC DEP 'The Bluebelt Program'; EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports

local.neighborhoodNote: Jamaica Bay (bordering southeast Brooklyn and southern Queens/the Rockaways) and the Gowanus Canal (Brooklyn) are the sharpest intra-city hot spots: both are enclosed, low-flushing waterbodies where nitrogen loading has historically driven hypoxia and salt-marsh loss, versus open, well-flushed reaches of the East River and Upper Bay where the Harbor Survey shows dissolved oxygen consistently meeting state standards. Jamaica Bay and its tributaries also carry by far the largest green-infrastructure footprint in the city — 994.8 of the 2,062 certified green/managed acres and 233.3 of the 680.7 MGY of certified CSO reduction as of December 2025. Sources: NYC DEP Jamaica Bay page, NYC DEP 2025 green infrastructure milestone certification, Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers timeline (https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/jamaica-bay.page, https://www.nyc.gov/assets/dep/downloads/pdf/water/stormwater/green-infrastructure/2025-green-infrastructure-milestone-certification.pdf, https://jamaicabayecowatchers.org/about-us/timeline-history-and-accomplishments/).

subIndicators.name: Citywide WRRF effluent total nitrogen load (all 14 facilities)
subIndicators.value: ~132,200 lb/day, equivalent to ~48.3 million lb/year or ~21,900 metric tons N/year, i.e. ~2.6 kg N/person/year at 8.26M residents. Reviewer-computed aggregate: sum across all 14 SPDES permits of the mean of the 12 CY2025 monthly-average Effluent Gross total-nitrogen quantities reported in EPA ECHO (parameter 00600). Per-plant CY2025 means, lb/day: Newtown Creek 26,342; North River 19,067; Owls Head 14,633; Wards Island 14,542; Bowery Bay 11,642; Oakwood Beach 9,017; Coney Island 8,108; Hunts Point 6,633; Jamaica 5,158; Tallman Island 4,892; Red Hook 4,801; Port Richmond 3,550; 26th Ward 2,617; Rockaway 1,242. Method caveats: plants report on differing statistical bases, and an unweighted mean of monthly averages is not a flow-weighted annual load. DEP and DEC publish no rolled-up citywide figure, so this is a derived number, not an agency publication.
subIndicators.source: EPA ECHO effluent charts, reviewer-computed from discharge monitoring reports for all 14 NYC WRRF SPDES permits

subIndicators.name: Long Island Sound nitrogen TMDL point-source load
subIndicators.value: Combined New York and Connecticut point-source load of 18,909 lb/day in 2025, a 68% reduction from the 2000 TMDL baseline of 59,000 trade-equalized lb/day, against a required 60% reduction — the target has been met and exceeded, first achieved in 2016 and still declining. NYC's four East River WRRFs (Wards Island, Hunts Point, Bowery Bay, Tallman Island) were upgraded to deliver this; DEP's most recent published figure for those four is a reduction of 'approximately 61 percent' (May 2018), and their CY2025 ECHO total is ~37,700 lb/day. Ecosystem-level targets such as eelgrass extent remain below goals.
subIndicators.source: Long Island Sound Partnership nitrogen loading indicator; NEIWPCC LIS TMDL program; NYC DEP press release 24 May 2018
subIndicators.geographicScale: regional (New York + Connecticut point sources discharging to Long Island Sound)

subIndicators.name: Jamaica Bay WRRF nitrogen loading trend
subIndicators.value: ~17,100 lb/day total nitrogen in CY2025 across the four Jamaica Bay WRRFs (26th Ward 2,617; Coney Island 8,108; Jamaica 5,158; Rockaway 1,242 — reviewer-computed from EPA ECHO DMRs), down from approximately 40,000 lb/day in early 2010 as stated by DEP. That is a ~57% reduction, meeting the 2010 Nitrogen Consent Agreement's target of 'more than 50% over 10 years'. The agreement committed $115M in total new investment, including ~$100M in WRRF nitrogen-control technology and ~$15M for marsh restoration.
subIndicators.source: EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports (current load, reviewer-computed); NYC DEP press release 7 February 2012 (2010 baseline and target)
subIndicators.geographicScale: city (four WRRFs discharging to Jamaica Bay)

subIndicators.name: Harbor-wide summer average dissolved oxygen
subIndicators.value: Above the NYS minimum standard of 5.0 mg/L every summer since the 1990s at open-water sites, surface and bottom, based on a ~40-site weekly Harbor Survey run since 1909
subIndicators.source: NYC DEP Harbor Survey Program / NYC Environment & Health Data Portal (portal not directly fetchable; wording confirmed via indexed text only)

subIndicators.name: Green infrastructure buildout and consent-order milestone status
subIndicators.value: DEP certified to DEC on 30 December 2025 that it had achieved a cumulative CSO volume reduction of 668 million gallons/year and a cumulative encumbrance of $1.4 billion — exactly the December 2025 milestone required by the 2023 order — and DEC's review of that certification was still open as of the Q1 2026 quarterly report. The underlying physical buildout is well behind the original trajectory: 2,062.0 green/managed acres as of 2025 against the ~8,000 acres implied by managing 1 inch of rainfall on 10% of impervious surface in combined sewer areas by 2030 (now 2040). DEP missed the 1.5%-by-2015 application-rate milestone and, in the 2023 order's own words, 'failed to achieve the 4% application rate by December 2020'; the 2023 modification replaced application-rate milestones with volume and dollar milestones and extended the 1.67 BGY endpoint from 2030 to December 2040, with a 2037 contingency plan and a December 2045 backstop.
subIndicators.source: NYC DEP 2025 green infrastructure milestone certification (30 Dec 2025); 2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Order on Consent (DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38); NYC DEP 2026 Q1 CSO quarterly report

subIndicators.name: Major CSO grey-infrastructure project timelines
subIndicators.value: Newtown Creek CSO Storage Tunnel: FEIS Notice of Completion 5 February 2026; City Council approved property acquisition 26 March 2026; ULURP complete 6 April 2026; NYC's first CSO storage tunnel. Flushing Bay: approved 25 MG tunnel replaced in DEP's December 2025 modification request by 6.5 MG in-line storage (complete Q2 2037) plus a 40 MG tunnel (complete Q4 2053), $3.42B total. Programme spending: ~$5.3B on CSO and green infrastructure 1995-2024, with ~$7.4B programmed 2025-2050, on top of ~$1.2B spent 1999-2022 upgrading 8 plants for biological nitrogen removal.
subIndicators.source: NYSDEC Environmental Notice Bulletin 18 Feb 2026; NYC DEP Flushing Bay LTCP public meeting 16 Dec 2025

global.levelRationale: Now anchored on published quantities rather than on directional judgement, which is what R2 requires. Anthropogenic nitrogen fixation stands at roughly 190 Tg N/year against a planetary boundary of 62 Tg N/year — a ~3.1x global overshoot, making biogeochemical flows one of the most transgressed boundaries. An equal-per-capita share of the 62 Tg boundary across ~8.1 billion people is ~7.7 kg N/person/year. Published per-capita footprints for the relevant population are 41 kg N/person/year for the US average (Leach et al. 2012, N-Calculator; of which ~30 kg is food production) and 30 kg N/person/year for Baltimore City, the closest published US municipal analysis. NYC residents therefore sit at roughly 3.9x to 5.3x their per-capita share — clearly beyond 'critical', below the ~5.5-6.9x overshoot that puts the climate global lens at 120. Confidence is medium, not high: no NYC-specific nitrogen footprint study exists, the transfer of a Baltimore/US per-capita figure to NYC is an extrapolation, and the equal-per-capita downscaling of the boundary is reviewer arithmetic on published numbers rather than a published benchmark. The score is not higher because a dense city with no agriculture, near-universal sewer connection and partial biological nutrient removal plausibly sits at the lower end of the US range; it is not lower because every credible per-capita figure for a US urban population is multiples of the fair share.
global.indicator: NYC residents' embodied/consumption-based nitrogen footprint, benchmarked against an equal-per-capita share of the planetary nitrogen boundary; with the US consumer phosphorus footprint as the phosphorus counterpart
global.value: No NYC-specific study exists. Best available anchors: US average per-capita nitrogen footprint 41 kg N/person/year, of which food production is ~30 kg (Leach et al. 2012, N-Calculator/N-Print). Baltimore City community nitrogen footprint 30 kg N/person/year, ~19,000 metric tons N total in 2016, 73% from food production — the closest published US municipal-scale analysis. US consumer phosphorus footprint 4.4 kg P/person/year, against a food-portion nitrogen footprint of 22.4 kg N/person/year, i.e. ~5.2 kg N released per kg P (Metson/Leach et al., Environ. Res. Lett. 2020). Applying the 30-41 kg N/person/year range to ~8.26M residents implies an order-of-magnitude footprint of roughly 250,000-340,000 metric tons N/year, and the 4.4 kg P figure implies roughly 36,000 metric tons P/year — both explicitly extrapolations from non-NYC per-capita figures, not measured NYC quantities.
global.target: No NYC-specific target exists. Planetary anchor: the biogeochemical flows boundary sets anthropogenic nitrogen fixation at 62 Tg N/year against a current value of ~190 Tg N/year, and the regional phosphorus flow boundary at 6.2 Tg P/year against ~18.2 Tg P/year (Planetary Health Check, after Richardson et al. 2023; Steffen et al. 2015 gave the same 62 Tg N boundary). An equal-per-capita share of the 62 Tg N boundary is ~7.7 kg N/person/year — reviewer-derived from the published boundary and world population, not a published downscaled benchmark.
global.context: NYC's nitrogen and phosphorus footprint is transmitted globally through its food system: importing produce, grain, meat and dairy from farms using synthetic nitrogen fertiliser manufactured from fossil gas and phosphate fertiliser from mined rock, a finite resource heavily concentrated in Morocco/Western Sahara. Roughly 19 billion pounds of food pass through the city each year, and household food consumption accounts for about 20% of the city's consumption-based greenhouse gas footprint — the same import dependence that drives the nitrogen footprint. The Baltimore City analysis (Environ. Res. Lett. 2020) shows this accounting is feasible at municipal scale and that the dominant term is food production (73%), with energy and transport a combined 15%; it also found substantial variation across census block groups driven by income and development, which is the equity handle for NYC. On the phosphorus side, the return loop is broken: DEP produces approximately 1,300 wet tons of dewatered biosolids a day (~475,000 wet tons/year) across its 14 WRRFs, was landfilling 100% as of 2010, and currently beneficially uses roughly 31% against a stated goal of diverting 100% from landfill by 2030. Every ton landfilled rather than land-applied is phosphorus not returned to agricultural soil, against a finite global phosphate-rock reserve. No NYC phosphorus-recovery programme (struvite precipitation or equivalent) was identified in any source consulted, so the recovery framing is real in principle but unquantified and unimplemented here.
global.source: Planetary Health Check / Richardson et al. 2023 (boundary values); Leach et al. 2012 N-Calculator (US per-capita N footprint); Deemer/Wang et al., 'A community nitrogen footprint analysis of Baltimore City, Maryland', Environ. Res. Lett. 15 075007 (2020); Metson/Leach et al., 'The U.S. consumer phosphorus footprint', Environ. Res. Lett. (2020); NEBRA reporting on NYC DEP biosolids (Mar 2024)

policyAnchors.name: 2023 Citywide Green Infrastructure Modification to the CSO Order on Consent (DEC Case No. CO2-20230228-38, effective 29 June 2023, modifying CO2-20000107-8)
policyAnchors.relevance: Sets the binding citywide CSO reduction target (1.67 billion gallons/year by December 2040 for the average rainfall year of 2008, combined sewer areas only, no MS4 credit) and the green infrastructure funding schedule ($1.4B encumbered by Dec 2025, $1.8B by Dec 2030, $2.8B by Dec 2035, $3.5B encumbered by Dec 2040, $3.5B expended by Dec 2045), with matching interim CSO volume milestones of 668 MGY, 700-800 MGY and 850-1,220 MGY. It replaced the 2012 order's impervious-acre application-rate milestones, which the city had missed at both 1.5% (2015) and 4% (2020). Quarterly progress reporting continues under the 2012 order's case number, CO2-20110512-25.
policyAnchors.status2026: Active. DEP certified the December 2025 milestone complete on 30 December 2025 (668 MGY, $1.4B encumbered); DEC issued comments in January 2026, DEP responded in March 2026, and DEC review remained open as of the Q1 2026 quarterly report published 30 April 2026. Major capital projects are moving: the Newtown Creek CSO Storage Tunnel FEIS Notice of Completion issued 5 February 2026, City Council approved property acquisition 26 March 2026, and ULURP completed 6 April 2026. The Flushing Bay modification request (6.5 MG in-line storage plus a 40 MG tunnel, $3.42B, completion Q2 2037 and Q4 2053) was submitted 31 December 2025 and is under DEC review; DEP told DEC it needed guidance before the end of May 2026 to proceed with in-line storage design.

policyAnchors.name: Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act (SPRTKA) enforcement — Matter of Riverkeeper v NYC DEP
policyAnchors.relevance: SPRTKA requires public notification of combined sewer overflow discharges within four hours; how fast residents learn of nitrogen- and pathogen-bearing discharges determines whether the CSO load translates into human exposure at the Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay and Jamaica Bay.
policyAnchors.status2026: Resolved against DEP and affirmed on appeal. The Supreme Court ruled in December 2023 that DEP had failed to notify the public as SPRTKA requires; the Appellate Division, Second Department affirmed in June 2026 (Matter of Riverkeeper, Inc. v New York City Dept. of Envtl. Protection, 2026 NY Slip Op 03444), granting mandamus to compel prompt public notification of untreated and partially untreated sewage discharges and holding that DEP's water quality advisories in their current form do not comply with SPRTKA. Petitioners were represented by the Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic on behalf of Riverkeeper, Save the Sound, Bronx Council for Environmental Quality, Newtown Creek Alliance, the NYC Water Trail Association, NY/NJ Baykeeper and Waterkeeper Alliance. Confidence medium: the slip opinion itself is not machine-fetchable and this rests on the reported citation and summary.

policyAnchors.name: Long Island Sound Nitrogen TMDL (2000 TMDL, EPA-approved 2001)
policyAnchors.relevance: The binding regional nutrient target NYC's East River WRRF upgrades were built to satisfy: a 60% reduction in point-source nitrogen from a baseline of 59,000 trade-equalized lb/day.
policyAnchors.status2026: Point-source target met and exceeded. The combined New York and Connecticut point-source load was 18,909 lb/day in 2025, a 68% reduction from baseline; the 60% goal was first met in 2016 and loads have continued to fall. Hypoxic area and volume in the Sound are trending down. Implementation continues under EPA's 2015 Nitrogen Reduction Strategy and New York's Long Island Nitrogen Action Plan (2015), and ecosystem-level targets such as eelgrass extent remain below goals — so the nutrient-loading requirement is complete while ecological recovery is not.

policyAnchors.name: 2010 Jamaica Bay Nitrogen Consent Agreement
policyAnchors.relevance: The $115M agreement (~$100M in WRRF nitrogen-control technology plus ~$15M for marsh restoration) that drove the Jamaica Bay nitrogen cuts, targeting a reduction of more than 50% over ten years from approximately 40,000 lb/day in early 2010.
policyAnchors.status2026: Target met. The four Jamaica Bay WRRFs averaged ~17,100 lb/day of total nitrogen in CY2025 per their own discharge monitoring reports, a ~57% reduction from the 2010 baseline. Component projects were delivered over 2012-2020: the 26th Ward carbon-addition facility (February 2012, >3,000 lb/day), $460M in upgrades at Jamaica and 26th Ward, and a $23M Rockaway upgrade (2018). Marsh and habitat work continues under the CSO order — ribbed mussel installation in Thurston Basin and Bergen Basin dredging certified design start in February 2026, and Spring Creek CSO facility tide gates entered full operation on 22 September 2025.

policyAnchors.name: NYS Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act (2022, $4.2B)
policyAnchors.relevance: A funding source explicitly eligible for CSO, stormwater and water-infrastructure projects (at least $200M for water infrastructure and at least $250M for stormwater and algal-bloom-related projects statewide), relevant to financing the $3.5B green infrastructure commitment.
policyAnchors.status2026: Passed by referendum in 2022; grant guideline documents were still being issued and revised into 2024, and the NY League of Conservation Voters published a 'three years on' status review. Implementation is ongoing rather than complete.

policyAnchors.name: NYC DEP Biosolids Beneficial Use Plan and 100%-landfill-diversion goal
policyAnchors.relevance: The phosphorus return loop: ~1,300 wet tons/day of biosolids, 100% landfilled as of 2010, currently ~31% beneficially used, against a goal of diverting 100% from landfill to beneficial use by 2030. Determines whether phosphorus collected from the city's food supply is returned to soil or buried.
policyAnchors.status2026: Active but well short of the goal; DEP has been soliciting beneficial-use partners. No NYC phosphorus-recovery (e.g. struvite) facility was identified. Current-year destination and landfill-versus-beneficial-use percentages could not be confirmed from a 2025/2026 primary DEP publication.

actions: Sign up for NYC DEP's Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act discharge notifications before swimming, boating or fishing in the Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay or Jamaica Bay — and hold DEP to the June 2026 Appellate Division ruling that its current advisories do not satisfy the four-hour notification requirement.

Comment during the Citywide (East River/Open Waters) and Jamaica Bay Long Term Control Plan public review processes (ltcp@dep.nyc.gov), and specifically on DEP's pending Flushing Bay modification request, which would push the CSO control tunnel's completion to Q4 2053.

Volunteer with Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers or the NY-NJ Harbor & Estuary Program on salt-marsh monitoring and restoration tied to the bay's nitrogen-loading history and the ribbed-mussel and basin-dredging work now underway under the CSO order.

Support DEP's transition to 100% beneficial reuse of biosolids by 2030 rather than landfilling, by following and commenting on DEP's Biosolids Beneficial Use Plan solicitations — this is the city's only live lever on phosphorus recovery, and it currently stands at roughly 31%.

Track and testify at the NYC Council Committee on Environmental Protection, Resiliency and Waterfronts on CSO-reduction reporting and green infrastructure funding, including the Council's own May 2025 finding that DEP's green infrastructure volume data is not published on NYC Open Data.

Cut household contributions to nutrient loads reaching CSO-affected waterways: keep lawn and garden fertiliser off paved surfaces and away from catch basins before rain, keep fats/oils/grease out of drains, and use the city's curbside organics collection so food waste is composted rather than adding nitrogen load at the treatment plant.
petalumaContrast: Petaluma's nitrogen and phosphorus story is groundwater nitrate near agricultural land and septic systems (most wells below the 10 mg/L drinking-water standard, with 4-7 mg/L hotspots near agricultural boundaries, scored level 20). NYC's is an engineered wastewater-and-CSO story roughly three orders of magnitude larger: approximately 18 billion gallons a year of combined sewage through 398 permitted outfalls, and 14 WRRFs discharging some 132,200 lb/day of total nitrogen (~21,900 t N/year) into an estuarine system. There is essentially no diffuse agricultural-runoff analog in NYC's version of this dimension, and no groundwater-nitrate analog either, since the city draws its water from upstate reservoirs rather than local wells. The structural difference cuts both ways: NYC's loading is concentrated at monitored point sources, which is why it has been cut by 57-68% under two enforceable nutrient targets that have both been met — a lever Petaluma's diffuse problem does not offer — while NYC's untreated wet-weather discharge has no Petaluma counterpart at all and is on a fix timeline running to 2053.
dataGaps: DEP and DEC publish no rolled-up citywide nitrogen (or phosphorus) loading total across the 14 WRRFs. This review built one from EPA ECHO discharge monitoring reports (~132,200 lb/day, CY2025), but it is a reviewer-computed unweighted mean of monthly averages, not a flow-weighted annual load and not an agency figure. NYC DEP's Bureau of Wastewater Treatment or NYSDEC's eDMR system holds the underlying data needed to do this properly.

The ~18 billion gallons/year headline carries no stated vintage. NYSDEC publishes it as an average with no year; DEP publishes no measured citywide annual total and normalises all LTCP modelling to the 'average rainfall year of 2008'. Competing figures do not reconcile: the State Comptroller reported 6.5 billion gallons of partially or untreated wastewater in FY2016-17, Riverkeeper's SPRTKA filings use 21 billion gallons through 460 outfalls, and Save the Sound uses 27 billion gallons. Most importantly, DEP's own 16 December 2025 Flushing Bay presentation shows an 'Untreated CSO Volume Reduction' graphic labelled 5.6 BGY (Baseline CSO & GI Program) and 3.5 BGY (LTCP CSO Program) that could not be reconciled with an 18 BGY total from the extracted slide text. Whether 18 BGY is a pre-programme baseline or a current modelled volume is unresolved and materially affects the level.

The outfall count needs a stated definition, not just a number. NYSDEC currently says 398 permitted CSO outfalls; its 2021 CSO Annual Report says 400 across the 12 of 14 WRRF sewersheds that are combined; the 2023 consent order recites 'approximately 418'; DEP's website says 700 combined sewer outfalls; advocacy filings use 460. These are different measures, not successive revisions.

No borough-aggregated CSO volume totals are published. DEP and DEC report by waterbody or drainage area (Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay, Flushing Creek, Jamaica Bay and Tributaries, Bronx River, Hutchinson River, Alley Creek, Coney Island Creek, Westchester Creek, East River/Open Waters), which only partially maps to boroughs and often spans two. Staten Island has no waterbody LTCP at all.

Current (2025/2026) biosolids destination and landfill-versus-beneficial-use percentages could not be confirmed from a primary DEP publication; the ~31% beneficial use / ~69% landfill split comes from 2024 reporting. The claim sometimes made that NYC historically land-applied biosolids out of state (Colorado, Florida, 1992-2010) could not be verified and has been removed. No NYC phosphorus-recovery programme was identified.

No NYC-specific nitrogen or phosphorus footprint study exists. The global lens uses the Baltimore City community nitrogen footprint (30 kg N/capita/yr) and the US national averages (41 kg N/capita/yr, 4.4 kg P/capita/yr) as explicitly labelled extrapolations, and downscales the 62 Tg N/yr boundary to a per-capita share by simple division — reviewer arithmetic, not a published benchmark. A CUNY or Columbia urban-metabolism group could do the NYC study; the Baltimore paper's method is directly transferable.

No NYC phosphorus loading series or phosphorus TMDL surfaced for the local lens. Nitrogen-weighting is correct for NYC's N-limited marine receiving waters (settled ruling), but a topic expert should confirm whether phosphorus deserves a separately sourced local sub-indicator, particularly for the freshwater and impoundment portions of the system.

26th Ward WRRF is in Significant/Category I Noncompliance with 9 quarters of significant noncompliance and repeated copper, TSS, silver and whole-effluent-toxicity exceedances (EPA ECHO, last inspection 11 March 2026). That is a chemical-pollution finding rather than a nutrient one and should be routed to the chemical pollution dimension.

questionsForOrchestrator: There is no accepted downscaled city-scale nitrogen-loading benchmark, and the planetary boundary's control variable (intentional N fixation) is a food-system input measure whose NYC share sits almost entirely in the consumption lens. R12 therefore cannot be applied mechanically to the LOCAL score the way it was for climate. Local 55 is anchored on the unabated share of the CSO load (1.67 BGY committed against ~18 BGY discharged) plus a ~50% citywide nitrogen removal efficiency, moderated by two met nutrient targets. Confirm this convention or supply a portrait-wide local N/P benchmark.

Under R6 the headline is CSO volume and under R10 borough values must measure the headline, so all five boroughs are value: null. That leaves 0 of 5 real borough values while genuine dated per-plant CY2025 nitrogen loads exist for all 14 WRRFs. Do you want a `boroughs` block on the citywide-WRRF-nitrogen subIndicator (the R7 pattern of carrying a figure on the entity it actually belongs to) so borough portraits can surface a real labelled number rather than only a note?

The citywide WRRF nitrogen total (~132,200 lb/day) is reviewer-computed from ECHO DMRs across 14 permits, with method stated and confidence capped at medium per R3. Confirm you want a derived aggregate carried in the dossier rather than left in dataGaps with DEP named as the holder.
